summary: Dehydroemetine is a synthetic analogue of emetine used as a tissue amoebicide for severe invasive amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery and amoebic liver abscess) when first-line nitroimidazoles (such as metronidazole or tinidazole) cannot be used or have failed. It is directly amoebicidal against the trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica, acting in tissue rather than the bowel lumen, so it must be followed by a luminal amoebicide (e.g. diloxanide furoate) to eradicate intestinal cysts. Dehydroemetine is less cardiotoxic and more rapidly excreted than emetine but still carries appreciable cardiac toxicity; it is given by deep intramuscular or subcutaneous injection (not intravenously) at about 1 mg/kg/day for the shortest effective course (commonly up to 4-5 days, not exceeding 10 days), with daily ECG, blood-pressure and pulse monitoring and bed rest. It is NOT FDA-approved and is largely of historical/limited use; this record is compiled from WHO/BNF and emetine-class pharmacology rather than a US label.

moa: Dehydroemetine is a tissue amoebicide that is directly lethal to the motile trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica. Like emetine, it inhibits protein synthesis by blocking ribosomal translocation (movement of the ribosome along messenger RNA), arresting peptide-chain elongation in the parasite. It acts on amoebae within the intestinal wall and in extraintestinal tissue (liver) rather than in the bowel lumen, so it does not reliably clear luminal cysts. Its cardiotoxic and neuromuscular effects reflect the same inhibition of protein synthesis in host tissues; dehydroemetine is cleared more rapidly than emetine, giving a somewhat better cardiac safety margin.

absolute: Pre-existing cardiac disease (cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, heart failure)

preg: Dehydroemetine crosses the placenta and is potentially embryotoxic; the emetine class is generally avoided in pregnancy. Use only if there is no safer alternative for a life-threatening invasive amoebic infection, under specialist supervision.
lact: There are insufficient data on dehydroemetine in breast milk. Because of its toxicity, breastfeeding is best avoided during treatment.
renal: Dehydroemetine is eliminated renally and can accumulate in renal impairment, increasing the risk of cardiotoxicity. Use with caution, reduce the dose, and monitor closely; avoid if possible in significant renal disease.
hepatic: Use with caution in significant hepatic disease. Although used to treat amoebic liver abscess, the drug's systemic toxicity warrants careful monitoring in patients with compromised hepatic function.

major: Other cardiotoxic or QT-prolonging drugs - additive cardiac toxicity; avoid
Neuromuscular blocking agents - additive neuromuscular weakness
moderate: Drugs that deplete potassium/magnesium - increased arrhythmia risk
interactions.diagnostics: Causes ECG changes (T-wave flattening/inversion, ST depression, QT prolongation); may raise muscle enzymes

common: Pain, tenderness or sterile abscess at the injection site
serious: Cardiotoxicity - ECG changes, arrhythmias, hypotension, precordial pain

Blood pressure and heart rate daily
Clinical response of the amoebic infection
counsel: This is a strong injectable medicine for a serious amoebic infection and is given under close monitoring
You will need to rest in bed and have daily heart tracing (ECG) and blood-pressure checks
Report chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness or marked muscle weakness immediately
A further (oral) medicine is needed afterwards to fully clear the infection from the bowel
Do not have alcohol and avoid strenuous activity during and shortly after treatment
Tell the team about any heart, kidney or muscle conditions you have
pk: Amoebicidal effect over the first days of therapy
Absorbed from IM/SC site; tissue concentrations build over the course
Eliminated more rapidly than emetine (shorter tissue persistence)

Store as per manufacturer; protect from light
pearls: NOT FDA-approved; a second-line/historical tissue amoebicide largely replaced by metronidazole/tinidazole - data here from WHO/BNF and emetine-class pharmacology
Tissue (not luminal) amoebicide - must be followed by a luminal agent such as diloxanide furoate to prevent relapse
Cardiotoxic: give deep IM/SC (never IV), enforce bed rest, and monitor ECG/BP/pulse daily
Less cardiotoxic and more rapidly excreted than emetine, but still hazardous
Avoid in cardiac and renal disease, pregnancy and the very young/elderly
Limit course length and do not repeat within ~6 weeks because of cumulative toxicity
missed: Doses are given by a healthcare professional as a supervised course, so a self-managed missed dose does not apply. If a scheduled dose is delayed, the treating team will adjust the regimen.
overdose: Overdose causes severe cardiotoxicity (arrhythmia, hypotension, heart failure) and neuromuscular weakness. There is no specific antidote; stop the drug, provide continuous cardiac monitoring and supportive care (treat arrhythmias and hypotension), and manage in a high-dependency setting.
